summary: Advises network administrators to remove old filters that blocked traffic or BGP routes from IPv4 /8 blocks that were once unallocated. Now that no unallocated /8s remain, such filters are fragile and costly. It lists the IPv4 prefixes that should still not be routed across the public Internet. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: People used to block mail from addresses nobody owned yet. Now every neighborhood has been handed out, so the old blocklist only causes mistakes. This says to throw it away.

questions: should i filter unallocated ipv4 space
ipv4 prefixes that should not be routed
subtitle: Stop blocking IPv4 address space that has now been fully allocated.

tldr.problem: Network administrators have filtered traffic from unallocated IPv4 address blocks to block bogus sources, but all IPv4 /8 blocks have now been allocated, making the filters fragile and likely to block legitimate traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Remove packet and BGP prefix filters that block traffic based on allocation status. Continue filtering only Martian prefixes reserved for special use by RFC 5735.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can simplify their border filters and avoid accidentally blocking valid traffic as address assignments change.

today: RFC 6441 remains current best practice guidance. Network operators who still maintain old bogon filters based on allocation status should remove them to avoid blocking legitimate traffic from newly assigned address space.

sections.title: Why Filters Became Obsolete
sections.content: For years, network administrators filtered traffic from and BGP prefixes of unallocated IPv4 address blocks. These bogon filters made sense when most of the address space was unallocated. However, all IPv4 /8 blocks are now allocated to regional registries. Continuing to filter based on allocation status is complex, fragile, and blocks legitimate traffic as assignments change daily.
sections.plainLanguage: When most addresses were unowned, filtering them was simple. Now that everything is owned, the filter just breaks things.

sections.title: What to Remove and What to Keep
sections.content: Network operators SHOULD remove both ingress and egress packet filters and BGP prefix filters for previously unallocated IPv4 /8s. The only filters worth keeping are for Martian prefixes—addresses reserved for special use by RFC 5735, such as loopback, private, and link-local ranges. These are defined in RFC 5735 and update processes ensure the list stays current.
sections.plainLanguage: Delete the filters for unallocated blocks. Keep only the ones for special addresses that are reserved forever, like your home Wi-Fi network.

sections.title: Security and Maintenance Benefits
sections.content: Removing obsolete filters simplifies network configuration and reduces operational costs. It also prevents accidental blocking of legitimate traffic from newly allocated address ranges. Network administrators maintaining old bogon filters face a fragile and expensive situation: they must update their filters daily as new address assignments happen, risking mistakes. Removing the filters based on allocation status while keeping filters for reserved special-use prefixes provides a cleaner, more maintainable approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Throwing away old filters is simpler and cheaper than trying to keep them up to date. And you will not accidentally block real customers.
